The asbF gene of Bacillus anthracis Sterne was cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli in two forms - one with a His6 tag fused to the N terminus, and a second with a cleavable tag fused to the C terminus. The proteins were purified, and used for in vitro biochemical analysis and for crystallization [Pfleger08].

The enzyme is dimeric, and has a requirement for divalent ions, with a preference for Mn2+. It's structure adopts a TIM barrel cofiguration, with the N terminus burried at the bottom part of the barrel [Pfleger08].

A homologous protein has been purified from Bacillus thuringiensis [] serovar konkukian str. 97-27 [Fox08a].

The protein provides an attractive drug target.

comment.text:
Corynebacterium glutamicum grows well with either L-quinate or shikimate as the sole carbon source [Teramoto09]. Disruption of qsuD, which encodes quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase, completely suppressed growth with either of these substrates but did not affect growth with glucose, indicating that the enzyme participates in the catabolism of quinate/shikimate but not in the biosynthetic shikimate pathway [Teramoto09].

Expression of the qsuD gene and the other genes in its operon is strongly induced during growth with either quinate or shikimate [Teramoto09].

The gene has been cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli and the recombinant protein was purified and characterized [Schoepe08]. The crystal structure has been sloved at 1.6 Å [Schoepe08]. The protein, which forms a homodimer in solution, has a lower Km for L-quinate than for shikimate, resulting in catalytic efficiency that is more than three times higher with the former.

The enzyme has a clear preference for NAD+ over NADP+. The turnover number decreases by more than 300-fold with NADP+ [Schoepe08].

comment.text:
YdiB was identified as a quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase. The low catalytic efficiency of YdiB with both quinate and shikimate suggests that neither may be the physiological substrate [Michel03]. Wild-type E. coli is not known to synthesize quinate or to use it as a source of carbon.

Phylogenomic analysis of the shikimate dehydrogenase family showed that the two enzymes encoded in E. coli, AroE and YdiB, belong to different subclasses; the authors suggested that YdiB was acquired by horizontal gene transfer. Common and subclass-specific catalytic residues and substrate binding motifs were identified [Singh08].

YdiB can use both NAD+ or NADP+ as a cosubstrate for catalysis [Michel03]. Because the intracellular concentration of NAD+ is 40-fold higher than that of NADH+, the dehydrogenase direction is expected to be favored by YdiB in vivo [Johansson06]. Conversely, AroE is NADP+- and substrate-specific and has much higher catalytic efficiency than YdiB [Michel03]. aroE mutant data and the results from metabolic engineering experiments strongly suggest that YdiB is unable to replace AroE under normal physiological conditions. Expression of YdiB for engineering of L-tyrosine production led to accumulation of the pathway intermediates dehydroquinate and dehydroshikimate and the side product quinate [Juminaga12].

Crystal structures of YdiB have been solved at 2.3 Å and 2.5 Å resolution [Benach03, Michel03]. Although AroE and YdiB have low sequence similarity, they have high structural similarity with two α/β domains separated by a wide cleft [Michel03]. Results from site-directed mutagenesis of predicted active-site residues do not support a general acid-base mechanism for catalysis [Lindner05].

Quinate is produced as a by-product in a genetically modified shikimate-producing E. coli strain [Draths99, Knop01] and can be attributed to YdiB activity [Garcia17a]. Expression of ydiB in a shikimate-producing strain is only induced under carbon-limiting growth conditions [Johansson06].

comment.text:
3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase catalyzes the dehydration of 3-dehydroshikimate to protocatechuate. The Neurospora crassa enzyme has been purified 1650-fold to homogeneity and found to be a monomeric protein of 37 kDa [Stroman78].

The purified enzyme was extremely sensitive to thermal denaturation, but was significantly stabilized by Mg2+ ions. In addition, maximal catalytic activity required the presence of a divalent cation, including Mg2+, Mo2+, Mn2+, Ba2+ and Co2+ [Stroman78].

The qa-4, which encodes the enzyme, has been isolated and sequenced [Rutledge84].

comment.text: The product of the qsuB gene of Corynebacterium glutamicum R has not been characterized. However, there are several reason to assume that it encodes dehydroshikimate dehydratase. First, the gene is present in an operon with other genes involved in the degradation of L-quinate and shikimate. Secondly, the amino-terminal half of the QsuB protein has 25% amino acid sequence identity to dehydroshikimate dehydratases identified in fungi, and thridly, the gene expression is induced during growth on L-quinate or shikimate. Curiously, the caroxy-terminal half of the enzyme has 25% amino acid sequence identity to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase [Teramoto09].

The quiC gene of Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 was found following the quiB gene within a single operon, which also contains the quiX gene. The quiC gene was cloned and sequenced, and had no close matches to sequences available at the time [Elsemore95]. The Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 gene was expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant cells had a specific 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase activity of 19.5 mmol/min/mg of protein [Elsemore95].

comment.text:
NAD+ and NADP+ are dinucleotides containing one nicotinamide base and one adenine base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety.

These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as cofactors. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".

The most common function of NAD+ is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts NAD+ to NADH, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.

NADPH, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of NADP+, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms NADP+ is reduced by photosystem I. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I).

comment.text:
General Background

Protocatechuate is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as vanillate and ferulate.

The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase and protocatechuate 2,3-dioxygenase. The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in protocatechuate degradation I (meta-cleavage pathway), protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway) and protocatechuate degradation III (para-cleavage pathway), respectively.

About This Pathway

The pathway that starts with protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase is part of a pathway known as the 3-oxoadipate pathway (or β-ketoadipate pathway). It is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi [Harwood96], although the pathway organization and regulation varies among species [Harwood96].

The β-ketoadipate pathway is comprised of two parallel branches, one branch converts protocatechuate to 3-oxoadipate and the other converts catechol to 3-oxoadipate. 3-oxoadipate is then converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, which are processed by the TCA cycle.

A variety of aromatic compounds, such as 4-hydroxybenzoate and benzoate, are shuttled into the respective protocatechuate and catechol branches of the β-ketoadipate pathway.

In Pseudomonas putida, all of the enzymes involved in protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway are inducible [Ornston66a]. Protocatechuate dioxygenase is induced by protocatechuate (as reported in [Harwood96], and the remaining five enzymes, 3-carboxymuconate cycloisomerase, 4-carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase, β-ketoadipate enol-lactone hydrolase, β-ketoadipate:succinyl-CoA transferase, and β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase are induced by β-ketoadipate [Ornston66a, Harwood96].

The genes that encode for the synthesis of the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of the protocatechuate branch of the β-ketoadipate pathway in P. putida are clustered into four distinct groups (as reported in [Harwood94]): pcaHG [Frazee93], pcaBDC [Williams92], pcaIJ [Parales93], and pcaRKF [Chan79]. In Acinetobacter calcoaceticus the genes are arranged in gene cluster pcaIJFBDKCHG that is induced by protocatechuate (as reported in [Harwood94]).

comment.text:
General Background

L-quinate is a naturally occuring compound found in decaying plant matter [Hawkins93]. Quinate is one of several aromatic compounds that can be metabolized by microorganisms to the central intermediate protocatechuate that can be further metabolized via the β-ketoadipate pathway to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA [Tresguerres70, Adachi03a]. Bacteria capable of using quinate as a sole carbon source were observed as early as 1911 [Beijerinck11]

Quinate degradation was initially studied in the fungus Neurospora crassa [Tatum54], and later in other fungi (such as Aspergillus nidulans [Hawkins85]) and bacteria, including Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 (at the time reported as Acinetobacter calcoaceticus) [Elsemore95, Elsemore94], Gluconobacter oxydans [Adachi03a] and Corynebacterium glutamicum [Schoepe08].| Many of these organisms can grow on quinate as a sole carbon and energy source, and the pathway is inducible by growth on either L-quinate, shikimate, or protocatechuate.

Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the main difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of L-quinate. Filamentous fungi and Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.1.24), while Gram-negative bacteria use a pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.99.25) [vanKleef88]. The later pathway is desribed in quinate degradation I.

About This Pathway

Quinate degradation was first studied in filamentous fungi such as Neurospora crassa and Aspergillus nidulans. The fungal pathway starts with conversion of L-quinate to 3-dehydroquinate by an NAD-dependent quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.24). The genes involved in the fungal pathway (qa genes in Neurospora crassa, qut genes in Aspergillus nidulans ) were shown to be present in a single cluster, and are induced by growth on either L-quinate or shikimate [Patel81, Wheeler96, Hawkins93]. The clusters include a gene encoding a permease that enables L-quinate to enter the organism [Whittington87].

An NAD-dependent enzyme is also present in certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as Corynebacterium glutamicum [Teramoto09]. As in the fungi, the qsuD gene, which encodes the Corynebacterium glutamicum enzyme, is located in a gene cluster that also contains the genes encoding the rest of the pathway's enzymes. The cluster, which is under the control of the QsuR regulator, is induced by growth on L-quinate shikimate [Teramoto09].

comment.text:
General Background

Shikimate is a common biosynthetic precursor of many compounds in microorganisms, higher plants, and animals (see chorismate biosynthesis I). As such, it is an abundant compound in the biosphere, and occurs commonly in decaying pant matter [Kramer03, Hawkins93].

In addition to its biosynthetic role, shikimate can be used by several microorganisms as a carbon and energy source. It is metabolized by two enzymatic reactions to protocatechuate, a central intermediate leading to complete mineralization (see protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway)).

Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of shikimate. Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD-dependent enzyme while Gram-negative bacteria use a pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.99.25) [vanKleef88]. The later pathway is desribed in shikimate degradation I.

About This Pathway

The Gram-Positive bacterium Corynebacterium glutamicum grows well with shikimate as the sole carbon source [Teramoto09]. This organism produces quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase, an NAD-dependent enzyme capable of using either L-quinate or shikimate as a substrate [Teramoto09, Schoepe08]. The 3-dehydroshikimate formed is dehydrated to protocatechuate by the enzyme dehydroshikimate dehydratase [Teramoto09].

The qsuD and qutB genes, which encode the pathway's enzymes, are present in a single operon that also includes qsuA and qsuC, which encode a quinate transporter and dehydroquinate dehydratase, respectively. The expression of the qsu genes is markedly induced during growth in the presence of either quinate or shikimate, and is regulated by the LysR-type transcriptional regulator QsuR [Teramoto09].

comment.text: Shikimate is an important intermediate in the chorismate biosynthetic pathway. It was first isolated from Japanese star anise. Shikimate is used for the production of some antiviral drugs used to halt the spread of the flu virus, but as a biosynthetic intermediate, it is usually not found in high concentrations in organisms. Shikimate can be easily harvested from the needles of several species of pine trees, and biosynthetic pathways in Escherichia coli have been enhanced to obtain sufficient amounts of the metabolite for commercial use.

comment.text:
General Background

Shikimate is a common biosynthetic precursor of many compounds in microorganisms, higher plants, and animals (see chorismate biosynthesis I). As such, it is an abundant compound in the biosphere, and occurs commonly in decaying pant matter [Kramer03, Hawkins93].

In addition to its biosynthetic role, shikimate can be used by several microorganisms as a carbon and energy source. It is metabolized by two enzymatic reactions to protocatechuate, a central intermediate leading to complete mineralization (see protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway)).

Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of shikimate. Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme while Gram-negative bacteria use a pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.99.25) [vanKleef88]. The former pathway is desribed in shikimate degradation II.

About This Pathway

The catabolic pathway of shikimate degradation has been documented in the Gram-negative bacterium Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1. This organism produces quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase (quinone), an enzyme capable of using either L-quinate or shikimate as a substrate [Elsemore94, Elsemore95, Adachi03]. While the bacterium Gluconobacter oxydans also produces a similar enzyme [Adachi03a], it is less active toward shikimate [Vangnai04]. In both organisms the enzyme is membrane-associated and requires pyrroloquinoline quinone as an electron acceptor.

The 3-dehydroshikimate formed is dehydrated to protocatechuate by the enzyme dehydroshikimate dehydratase [Elsemore95].

The pathway is inducible by growth on quinate, shikimate, or protocatechuate [vanKleef88]. In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 the qui genes for quinate degradation and the pca genes for protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway are organized into a large transcriptional unit [Barbe04, Dal05].
